paragraphs.heading: Heart, vessels and blood
paragraphs.text: In vertebrates, the circulatory system is a set of organs: the heart, the blood vessels, and the blood that is moved through all of them. The heart and the vessels together are called the cardiovascular system, a name built from a Greek word for heart and a Latin word for vessels. Some writers treat the terms cardiovascular system, vascular system and circulatory system as meaning the same thing.

paragraphs.heading: Two loops
paragraphs.text: The system runs as two circuits. The pulmonary circulation takes blood that has lost its oxygen from the right side of the heart to the lungs, where it is oxygenated, and brings it back to the left side. The systemic circulation sends that oxygen-rich blood from the left heart through the aorta to the rest of the body. Two large veins, the superior and inferior venae cavae, then return the used blood to the right heart. To serve both loops, the human heart has four chambers: one atrium and one ventricle for each circuit.

paragraphs.heading: A closed network
paragraphs.text: The vessels range from the great vessels of the heart, such as large elastic arteries and big veins, down to smaller arterioles, capillaries, and small veins called venules. In vertebrates the system is closed, which means the blood never leaves this network of vessels. Nutrients reach the organs through the tiny vessels of the microcirculation. Many invertebrates, such as arthropods, work another way: their heart pumps a fluid called hemolymph that comes back through the body cavity instead of through vessels. Sponges and comb jellies have no circulatory system at all.

paragraphs.heading: What the blood carries
paragraphs.text: Blood is a fluid in which red cells, white cells and platelets float in plasma. As it travels it brings oxygen and nutrients to the tissues and collects waste to be disposed of. Among the things it carries are proteins, minerals, hormones and hemoglobin, as well as gases like oxygen and carbon dioxide. These substances nourish the body, help the immune system fight disease, and keep temperature and pH steady. An average adult holds five to six quarts of blood, about 7% of total body weight.

paragraphs.heading: The lymphatic partner
paragraphs.text: In vertebrates, the lymphatic system works alongside the circulatory system. Some plasma is filtered out of the capillaries into the spaces between cells, and lymphatic vessels gather up this extra fluid and return it to the blood as lymph. Without this return route, the blood would run short of fluid. Lymph moves much more slowly than blood, and unlike the closed blood system, the lymphatic system is open. It also works with the immune system to defend the body against pathogens.

paragraphs.heading: Side routes and specialists
paragraphs.text: Besides the two main loops, there are routes that serve particular organs, such as the coronary circulation, which supplies the heart itself, plus cerebral circulation for the brain and renal circulation for the kidneys. Many cardiovascular diseases can affect the system. Cardiologists specialise in the heart, cardiothoracic surgeons operate on the heart and the area around it, and vascular surgeons treat disorders of the blood vessels and lymphatic vessels.
